teaser: Monet turned 800 years of carved stone into a few minutes of sunshine.
review_notes:
Lichtenstein's Rouen Cathedral series dated 1969: confirm.
Monet working in the fitting room of a ladies' clothing shop behind a screen: well-known anecdote, check wording.
'More than thirty' canvases; twenty shown at Durand-Ruel in May 1895.
Nightmare of the cathedral falling on him (blue, pink or yellow) comes from a letter to Alice Hoschedé.
The idea that the motif mattered less than what lay between him and it is a paraphrase of a remark reported in 1895, not a direct quote.
Clemenceau's article 'Révolution de cathédrales' (1895) and his call for the state to buy the series.
Museum counts: National Gallery of Art owns two, Musée d'Orsay five.
The three small dabs at bottom left are read here as passers-by; check against the painting.

lesson.text: In 1969 the American Pop artist Roy Lichtenstein made a set of pictures of one church front. Same outline every time, printed in mechanical dots, once in yellow, once in red and blue, once almost black. He was quoting this painting and its sisters. Lichtenstein had spotted something very modern in them: an image repeated like a product, with only the color switched.

Monet got there seventy-five years earlier. In the late winters of 1892 and 1893 he rented rooms facing the west front of Rouen Cathedral, in Normandy, and painted it more than thirty times. He kept many canvases going at once and moved from one to the next as the day advanced. This is one of the sunniest.
One of his makeshift studios was the fitting room of a ladies' clothing shop across the square. Customers complained about the man with the paintbrushes, so a screen was put up to hide him.

From that window Monet was so close that the building does not fit. The towers are cut off on both sides and at the top, and there is hardly any ground. Without a street or a horizon, how can you tell how big this thing is? He left one clue, right at the bottom.
Somebody is walking past the cathedral. Find the passers-by.

spots.title: Three people
spots.text: Three dabs of mauve, blue and green, each a couple of brushstrokes tall. They are figures on the square. Measure the doors against them and the facade becomes a cliff.

lesson.text: Those three specks are the only living things in the picture. Monet did not care about the saints carved over the doors or about the services held inside. He treated one of the great Gothic churches of France, built from the 1100s onward, exactly as he had treated a pile of wheat in a field: as a surface for light to land on.

And yet the paint itself behaves like stone. Monet dragged layer over layer of thick, dry color until the surface became rough and crusty, a little like weathered limestone. Paint laid on this thickly is called impasto. In a museum, the ridges catch the gallery lights just as the real carvings catch the sun.
The work wore him down. He wrote home that he had a nightmare in which the cathedral collapsed on top of him, and that it seemed to be blue, or pink, or yellow.

So what was he chasing so hard? He once explained that the subject itself hardly mattered to him. What he wanted to paint was whatever lay between the subject and his eye: the air, the haze, the glare. Wander over the facade and see where that air turns blue and where it turns gold.

spots.title: The sky
spots.text: The only calm, flat area in the picture. This strong blue is what makes the stone beside it look so hot and white.

spots.title: The great arch
spots.text: The deep hollow above the main door is in shade. Monet paints it violet, blue and dull gold. A shadow here is cool air, never a dark hole.

spots.title: The rose window
spots.text: A Gothic rose window is a huge round window filled with stone tracery. Here it is a soft swirl of blue, pink and ochre with no drawn spokes at all.

spots.title: The central door
spots.text: The deep doorway glows orange and pink, warmed by sunlight bouncing up from the pavement of the square.

spots.title: Blue on the tower
spots.text: Long streaks of sky blue run down the left tower. They are the shaded sides of its buttresses, the stone supports that stick out from the wall.

spots.title: Signed and dated
spots.text: “Claude Monet 94.” He began the canvas in Rouen but kept reworking it in his studio at Giverny, and only dated the series when he let it go.

lesson.text: A series does not show a thing. It shows time passing over a thing. The cathedral never changes; the hour, the weather and the air in front of it never stop changing.

Monet reworked the canvases at home in Giverny for more than a year. In May 1895 he hung twenty of them together in a Paris gallery. His friend Georges Clemenceau, a journalist who would later lead France as prime minister, wrote a front-page article begging the government to buy the whole set so it could stay together. Nobody listened.
The cathedrals were sold one at a time and are now scattered across the world. The Musée d'Orsay in Paris has five. The National Gallery of Art in Washington has two, including this one.

Which brings us back to Lichtenstein and his dots. He understood that no single cathedral is the work. The work is the difference between one and the next. If you ever stand in front of two of them, spend your time on the gap.

quiz.question: Which later artist quoted Monet's cathedrals in printed dots?
quiz.explanation: Lichtenstein made his own Rouen Cathedral sets in 1969.

quiz.question: Why are the cathedral's towers cut off by the frame?
options: He painted from a window very close to the building
quiz.explanation: From rooms across the square the facade was too close to fit.

quiz.question: What does the word impasto mean?
quiz.explanation: The thick, crusty paint of this canvas is a good example.

quiz.question: What gives the viewer a sense of the building's size?
options: Three tiny figures at the bottom left
quiz.explanation: Three dabs of color stand for people on the square.

quiz.question: What did Georges Clemenceau ask the French government to do?
quiz.explanation: He wanted the set kept together, but the state did not act.

quiz.question: According to Monet, what was he really trying to paint?
options: The religious meaning of the church
Every carved detail of the stone
What lay between the subject and his eye
quiz.explanation: The air and light in front of the building mattered more to him than the building.

facts.text: Monet painted the cathedral series entirely outdoors on the square.
facts.explanation: He worked from rented rooms facing the facade and finished the canvases in his Giverny studio.

facts.text: One of Monet's Rouen studios was the fitting room of a clothing shop.
facts.explanation: A screen was set up there to hide him from the customers.

facts.text: The French state bought all twenty cathedrals shown in 1895.
facts.explanation: Despite Clemenceau's appeal, they were sold separately and scattered.
